rationale: B wins because its proof gates are sharper and more useful to a founder deciding what not to pitch yet. Its line, "If there is none, say so before pitching; the reporter will ask," is the adult in the room. A is strong, but "Why athletes and biohackers are the test market for blood-oxygen sleep tracking" turns a marketing audience into a test-market claim without evidence.
gaps_in_A: "Why athletes and biohackers are the test market" overclaims from the supplied fact that Eight Sleep markets to athletes and biohackers; marketing target is not proof of a test market.

"The story is what this audience actually does with the data" is the right question, but A keeps the angle before it has a named user or usage data. That is a feature idea wearing a customer-story hat.
"the prevailing belief is 'if a device measures clinical signals, it's basically a health tool'" invents a broad public belief. The regulatory angle works without decorating it.
A refuses clinic puffery correctly, but misses the narrower conditional clinic angle: study design, funding, endpoints, and whether the investigator will speak before results exist.
gaps_in_B: "the moment the reading appears on a customer's phone" invents a phone/app surface not present in the update. Same problem with "what the app tells a user" and "What does the app show".

"A sleep clinic agreed to study a consumer mattress. Here is what it is measuring." is thin now; B says there are no results, then still keeps it as a pitchable angle. That needs PI access and study documents before it earns an inbox.
"category-creation" is grander than the facts support. This is a closed-loop product angle, not proof that Eight Sleep created a category.
"The company markets to athletes and biohackers" is bolted onto the closed-loop angle's facts even though the angle itself is not about that audience. Loose sourcing is how slop sneaks back in.
